  3. The ECMAScript runtime (src/engine/jsrt)

#The ECMAScript runtime (src/engine/jsrt)

The runtime is the "second half" of Wren's Odin JavaScript engine: it executes QuickJS‑ng 0.17 bytecode. It is written natively in Odin, builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with an injected allocator and no OS dependency, and runs inside Wren's Wasm sandbox exactly as QuickJS‑in‑Wasm does (the sandbox is kept on purpose: it protects the host from memory bugs of the engine).

The two halves of the engine meet at the QuickJS‑ng 0.17 bytecode: the Odin front‑end (frontend.md) and the reference QuickJS C compiler emit the same serialized form, and this runtime reads and runs it. compile_frontend.odin calls the front‑end in process (a scratch arena per compile), so eval, Function(...), modules and $262.evalScript need no other compiler.

This is not a mechanical port of QuickJS. Where the C uses #define tags, manual refcounting and hand‑rolled dispatch, the Odin version uses tagged unions with exhaustive switch, defer, arenas where they help, comptime‑generated opcode/atom tables, and layouts friendly to #soa. Divergences are deliberate and listed at the end.

#Conformance (test262)

tools/jsrt_test262.ps1 builds the judge (src/engine/jsrt/judge) and runs the suite pinned by tools/test262.ps1 in worker processes (a crash or hang costs one test), with the rules of QuickJS‑ng's test262.conf. The harness files and the includes / flags of each test's front matter are honoured (onlyStrict, raw, async, module, CanBlockIsFalse); $262 provides createRealm, evalScript, detachArrayBuffer, gc, IsHTMLDDA and real agents (threads with their own runtime, sharing SharedArrayBuffer memory; Atomics.wait/notify go through a process‑wide waiter list).

The 34 failures are the tests QuickJS‑ng itself fails: evaluation order of destructuring targets (7), callexpression as an assignment target (7, Annex B), AsyncFromSyncIterator close on poisoned wrappers (6), ambiguous export * namespaces (4), top‑level‑await ordering (2), using in imported modules (3), field named get/set followed by a generator (2), with over a proxy environment (2), and a few single cases. The full list is in build/test262/jsrt_errors.txt; every directory is at 100 % of what QuickJS‑ng passes.

#Value model (value.odin)

A Value is a 16‑byte tagged union: an 8‑bit Tag plus an 8‑byte payload (int32, float64, bool or a pointer to a GC cell). A tagged union rather than NaN‑boxing, on purpose:

  • It is identical on 64‑bit native and on wasm32; every switch v.tag is checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler.
  • Small integers stay unboxed (int32, as QuickJS); -0, non‑integral and out‑of‑range numbers use the float64 lane.

Heap values (string, symbol, object, bigint, raw function bytecode, module) hold a ^Cell. The representation is isolated behind constructors/accessors. The C API layer (below) encodes a Value in the 64‑bit NaN‑boxed word QuickJS uses on wasm32, because Wren's glue is written against that.

#Strings, atoms, shapes, objects

  • Strings (string.odin): UTF‑16 code units stored compactly — Latin‑1 (one byte per unit) or UTF‑16 — with ropes for concatenation (a + b + c… in a loop is linear; flattened on first index/hash/compare). Source text handed to the compiler keeps lone surrogates (WTF‑8), and Function.prototype.toString returns the real source text (the front‑end keeps each function's text with Compile_Options.keep_source; Host_Config.strip_source drops it).
  • Atoms (atom.odin, atoms_table.odin): 32‑bit interned property keys; array indices set bit 31 and never allocate. The predefined atoms are generated from quickjs-atom.h, so serialized bytecode refers to the same indices. Atoms are never collected.
  • Shapes (shape.odin/object.odin): hidden classes with transitions and an open‑addressed hash; an object stores a flat []Prop_Slot; deleting a property or growing past 48 properties switches the object to a private dictionary shape.
  • Objects: a GC cell with a shape, inline slots, and an Object_Data tagged union for the internal slots of exotic kinds (Array, Function, Native, Bound, wrappers, ArrayBuffer/TypedArray/DataView, Map/Set, Proxy, Date, RegExp, Promise, Generator, Module namespace, Host…). Arrays keep a dense []Value fast path.

#Memory management (gc.odin)

A precise, non‑moving, stop‑the‑world mark‑and‑sweep collector (rt.cells is every live cell). Copying a Value is a plain copy: there are no dup/free pairs in the interpreter and cycles need no special pass.

  • Roots: realms, the interpreter frame chain (arguments, locals, whole operand stacks, open closure cells), the job queue, the pending exception, atoms, the module registry, temp_roots, and the host roots (below).
  • Safe points (function entry, loop back edge, entry of a native call) are the only places a collection starts; allocation never collects. Native code (builtins) keeps Values in Odin locals the collector cannot see; cell_new and get/call push what they return on temp_roots, which a native call truncates when it returns. Builtins that read straight out of internal storage and then call back into JS root explicitly (root).
  • Weak references (WeakMap/WeakSet keys, WeakRef, FinalizationRegistry) are ephemerons processed to a fixpoint after the strong marking; shape transition caches are weak too.
  • Host roots: each Cell has a 32‑bit ext count. persist/ext_ref bump it (O(1), no table), unpersist/ext_unref drop it; cells with a non‑zero count are listed in rt.ext_cells and are roots.
  • Host classes (host_class.odin): objects of a class the host registers carry an opaque pointer, a finalizer, and optionally the references the opaque data holds (gc_mark) and exotic hooks for properties the object does not store. Finalizers of dead host objects run before any cell of the collection is freed. gc_mark is used twice: to subtract those references from the host counts (a cycle through opaque data does not keep itself alive — QuickJS's trial deletion, restricted to the cells with host references) and to trace them when the owner is live.
  • Small blocks (≤ 512 bytes: cells, inline slots, small arrays and string data) come from size‑class free lists carved out of 256 KiB chunks of the injected allocator (mem_alloc / mem_free / mem_resize in gc.odin; callers always pass the size they allocated with). A cell costs a pop and a push, not a host allocation.
  • The heap is capped by Host_Config.malloc_limit; all allocation goes through the injected allocator. A collection runs when the heap passes max(2 × live, live + 4 MiB).

#Where the memory of a realm and of a page goes (Wasm, jsengine mem|startup)

The linear memory of a Wasm module only grows, so what counts is the high-water mark.

  • Lazy members. A Web IDL prototype (native/js/odin/wj/qjs_platform.odin, wj_platform_preinit) is marked lazy with JS_SetLazyMembers: its shape is private and flagged, and shape_find, the enumerations of a shape (own_property_keys, plain_keys_object) and add_property call shape_realize first, which runs the glue's callback (lazy_proto_members): it defines the members the eager code defined, with the same keys, order, descriptors, names and lengths, minus what the realm's scope hides and the touch handlers browser.touch.expose turned off, plus the unimplemented-throw members after the implemented ones. A realm creates the thousands of function objects of the interfaces a script looks at, not all of them. A prototype that pre-initialization touches after the members (iterator interfaces) is realized in the image. The interface objects, namespaces and the global object stay eager. Empty realm: 6 592 → 4 352 KiB of linear memory, 6 973 → 4 723 KiB private per realm, 2.3 → 1.3 ms to create.
  • Native functions. A function object has exactly the two slots (length, name) it is born with; a C function of the glue without user data keeps its pointer in Native_Data.data (low bit set, native_data_is_raw) and its prototype in which bridge_* procedure it calls (no block of values); its name is the string of the property key's atom when there is one (str_interned).
  • The compiler (compile_alloc.odin): the front-end's allocator takes blocks up to 2 KiB from the arena, recycles them by size class (a larger free block is cut for a smaller request), and takes larger ones from the host heap, one by one, so that a table that dies is given back at once. js_create_function frees a function's tables (free_func_def) as soon as its bytecode exists, the passes free their buffers, and the serialized stream is built in one buffer (serialize.odin). The 650 KiB bundle of examples/jsbench/page_gen.js asked the arena for 14.6 MB, now 6.5.

#Serialized‑bytecode reader and verifier (serialize.odin)

Parses JS_WriteObject(..., JS_WRITE_OBJ_BYTECODE) for BC_VERSION 28: header, atom table (both atom encodings of the format), function bytecode (flags, vardefs, closure vars, cpool, bytecode, debug info, source), BigInt, arrays, objects, modules. After the instruction stream is read, its atom operands are rewritten in place and a stack‑height verifier checks the code. The interpreter trusts the types of operands (as QuickJS does: bytecode comes from the compiler); the reader and verifier guarantee shape and stack discipline, not type correctness.

#Interpreter (interp.odin, ops.odin, coro.odin)

A switch‑dispatch loop over the QuickJS instruction set. The common instructions (locals, arguments, integer / float arithmetic, comparisons, branches, get_field / put_field with the prototype walk, array reads and writes, global variables through a per‑realm slot cache, calls and returns) run in interp_hot.odin, a loop with raw pointers whose few live values stay in registers; everything else, and every fast path that does not apply, leaves it with the pc on the instruction for the full dispatch in interp.odin. The hot loop is inlined into interp_run (measured: a separate procedure is 20‑25 % slower). Frames come from segmented value stacks so generators and async functions can suspend them (coro.odin: generators, async functions, async generators, for await, yield*). A plain JS‑to‑JS call does not recurse natively: frame_push puts the callee's Frame at the end of its value‑stack block and the same interp_run activation runs it (Frame.stackless); native callees (c_function) are called from the hot loop without a frame. The engine's own stack budget and call depth bound recursion (Host_Config.max_stack_bytes, max_stack_depth; a RangeError instead of a crash). The interrupt hook runs on a budget from the loop back edge. Operators follow the spec (+ through ToPrimitive, ModRing bitwise, BigInt paths, loose and strict equality). Try/catch uses a per‑frame handler stack (catch/gosub/ret/nip_catch).

#Standard library

Everything QuickJS‑ng 0.17 ships, in b_*.odin: Object, Function, Array, String (with Unicode case mapping and normalization from src/engine/unicode), Number/Math/BigInt (numconv, bigint), Symbol, JSON (with source text access), RegExp, Date (datetime), Map/Set/WeakMap/WeakSet/WeakRef/ FinalizationRegistry, Promise, generators, Reflect/Proxy, ArrayBuffer (resizable, immutable)/ SharedArrayBuffer (growable)/TypedArray/Float16Array/DataView/Atomics, Iterator helpers and Iterator.concat, Array.fromAsync, DisposableStack/AsyncDisposableStack/SuppressedError, Uint8Array base64/hex, Error.prototype.stack. Intl stays on the host (Wren's glue).

Regular expressions. Literals reach the runtime already compiled by the front‑end to the bytecode of QuickJS's libregexp; lre_exec.odin executes that format (and a verifier checks it before use), so literals and new RegExp share one matcher. Unicode properties, case folding and the properties of strings (\p{RGI_Emoji} …) come from tables generated from the pinned UCD.

#Embedding interface (embed.odin, runtime.odin)

engine_new / context_new / eval_source / eval_bytecode / call_function / run_jobs / retain / release / heap_stats, with the hooks in Host_Config: compile, load_module, import_meta, interrupt, rejection, gc_prologue, compile_strings, dynamic_import, atomics_wait/atomics_notify, can_block, malloc_limit. Values handed to the host live until the next call into the engine unless retained.

src/engine/jsrt/wasm is the freestanding module (jsrt_init/new/alloc/eval/run_jobs/free).

#The QuickJS C API on this runtime (src/engine/jscapi)

Wren's glue is written against quickjs.h. jscapi implements that API (167 procedures, proc "c", exported under their QuickJS names with -define:JSCAPI_EXPORT=true) over jsrt; see jscapi.md for the ownership model, the classes and the plan of what is left.

#Measurements (Windows x64, Odin -o:speed, Zig 0.15 -O2 for QuickJS)

tools/jsrt_bench.ps1 produces the speed table; tools/jsrt_ab.ps1 compares several builds (and QuickJS) interleaved, best of N, on micro.js or macro.js; tools/jsrt_prof.ps1 is a sampling profiler (hot functions and source lines; JSRT_PROF=1 on judge eval); tools/jsrt_mem.ps1 measures the peak working set. JSRT_MEMPROF=1 on judge eval prints a census of the heap by kind of cell (count, cell bytes, bytes owned out of line, slack; memprof.odin), jsengine mem [-image m.wasm] file.js does the same inside the wasm32 image (sizes of the cells on wasm32, linear memory of the module, which only grows), and WREN_JS_MEMPROF=1 makes jsdomtest print it for each page. examples/jsbench/page_gen.js generates a 650 KB framework-like bundle for page-load memory (the compile arena dominates it). Timings on this machine swing by ±30 % from run to run when other builds are running, and a change that adds no work to the hot loop can still move an unrelated case by ±10 % (code layout), so compare interleaved and keep the best. Fuzzing: judge fuzz <dir> mutates serialized bytecode and loads it (reader + verifier; 40 000 mutants, no crash; running accepted mutants is opt‑in with JSRT_FUZZ_RUN=1, since a type‑confused image can crash any interpreter that trusts the compiler); judge fuzzsrc <dir> mutates source text, compiles with the Odin front‑end and runs under an interrupt budget (30 000 mutants on language/ and built-ins/, no crash).

#Intended divergences from QuickJS

  • Tagged union over NaN‑boxing for values; precise tracing GC instead of reference counting plus a cycle collector (the C API layer re‑creates the counted‑reference contract for the glue).
  • Exhaustive Odin enums + switch for tags, exotic kinds and opcodes; comptime‑generated opcode and atom tables from the QuickJS headers.
  • Rope strings with Latin‑1/UTF‑16 compaction as the default string representation.
  • Atoms are permanent; JS_WriteObject of data (structured clone format) is not implemented.

#Known gaps

The 34 test262 failures above (all shared with QuickJS‑ng). Speed is at parity with QuickJS on the micro benchmarks; the slow cases are the ones that pay one dispatch per bytecode (switch on integers 62 %, nested integer loops 69 %: next step is superinstructions or a pre‑decoded code array), native‑to‑JS callbacks (sort comparators, forEach: a new interp_run activation each, ~1.9× slower than QuickJS) and destructuring. Memory is 1.4× QuickJS on allocation‑heavy scripts (a plain object costs 168 bytes: Object 104 + 4 inline slots; a string header is 80 bytes; both can shrink).
